vignette:
Kwasi, a 25-year-old journalist, had always approached the world with an open curiosity, a drive to tell stories that mattered. That changed one sweltering evening nine months ago. He had been covering a community vigil in his neighborhood, the air thick with shared grief and defiant hope. As people began to disperse, a sudden surge of police vehicles descended, sirens wailing, lights flashing. Kwasi, caught in the crowd, found himself shoved against a wall, his camera snatched, his identification ignored. The memory of the officer's heavy boots thudding closer on the pavement, the shouts, and the disorienting blast of a car stereo nearby playing a specific, insistent rap song, was seared into his mind. He was detained for hours, interrogated, and released without charges, but the feeling of being completely powerless, stripped of his dignity and his voice, never left him.

In the months that followed, Kwasi found his world shrinking. The moments from that night felt more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, often intruding without warning. When he tried to talk about it, to his partner or even to his editor, he would lose the thread, the words catching in his throat, unable to finish explaining what had happened. He'd find himself back in that alley, the thud of approaching footsteps echoing in his head, even when he was alone in his apartment. Now, any sound of footsteps behind him on the street or in the office hallway would send a jolt of panic through him. If he heard that particular rap song, even faintly from a passing car, his heart would race, and a cold sweat would break out, transporting him back to the helplessness of that night.

His work, which once defined him, became a source of immense struggle. He found himself having difficulty concentrating on articles, the words blurring on the screen, his thoughts constantly drifting to potential threats. The investigative pieces that required him to venture into unfamiliar neighborhoods, to meet sources in new places, now felt impossible. He would avoid going to unfamiliar places, convinced he could not properly assess the danger. What if he was caught off guard again? What if another trauma-related event unfolded, and he was once again powerless? He started wearing concealing clothing - hoodies, baseball caps pulled low - hoping to blend in, to avoid being noticed, to make himself less of a target. He had come to believe that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him as a journalist, as a man.

The constant vigilance exhausted him. Walking anywhere, he frequently looked behind him to check if someone was following, his neck stiff with tension. He used to be a happy person, but now he was always miserable, a heavy shroud of despair settling over him. He started avoiding anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, a numb indifference becoming his default. This emotional distance began to strain his relationship, his partner struggling to understand his sudden withdrawal. He also found himself avoiding anything that reminded him of the profound loss of his former self, the injustice he had witnessed, and the person he used to be - the vibrant, engaged Kwasi.

The final straw came when he missed a crucial deadline for a story he'd once been passionate about, unable to focus, paralyzed by the fear of leaving his apartment to conduct interviews. He sat at his desk, staring at a blank screen, the weight of his unwritten future pressing down on him. He felt utterly broken, his career, his relationship, his very identity slipping away. He knew then that he couldn't continue this way, that the person he was disappearing, leaving behind only fear and despair. What frightened him most was the thought that this hollowed-out version of himself was all that remained. He needed help to find his way back, to reclaim the life he felt had been stolen.
